                                   1

                                   2

                                   3

                                   4                                  UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                                 NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6

                                   7     SEMICONDUCTOR GLOBAL                              Case No. 25-cv-04075-HSG
                                         SOLUTIONS,
                                   8                                                       ORDER DENYING MOTION FOR
                                                        Plaintiff,                         PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION AND
                                   9                                                       MOTION TO DEPOSIT FUNDS
                                                 v.
                                  10                                                       Re: Dkt. No. 68
                                         CAPITAL ASSET EXCHANGE AND
                                  11     TRADING, LLC, et al.,
                                  12                    Defendants.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13

                                  14          Pending before the Court is a motion for preliminary injunction filed by Plaintiff

                                  15   Semiconductor Global Solutions (“Plaintiff” or “SGS”). Dkt. No. 68. The Court finds this matter

                                  16   appropriate for disposition without oral argument and the matter is deemed submitted. See Civil

                                  17   L.R. 7-1(b). For the reasons detailed below, the Court DENIES the motion.

                                  18     I.   BACKGROUND
                                  19          In 2022, Plaintiff, a Chinese corporation, purchased semiconductor manufacturing

                                  20   equipment from Defendant Capital Asset Exchange & Trading LLC (“CAET”) for $2 million.

                                  21   Defendant CAET, for its part, does not appear to dispute that it received these funds and has not

                                  22   delivered the equipment. Rather, CAET contends that it cannot return the funds until it has

                                  23   authorization to do so from the United States Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign

                                  24   Assets Control (“OFAC”). See, e.g., Dkt. No. 72 at 1 (“CAET determined it could not lawfully

                                  25   deliver the Equipment to SGS” and “could not refund SGS’s payment either, at least [not] without

                                  26   a license from the appropriate regulatory agency”). Specifically, CAET argues that SGS is owned

                                  27   by a subsidiary of Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (“SMIC”), which

                                  28   appears on a list of entities that OFAC has determined pose a risk to U.S. national security. Id. In
                                         Case 4:25-cv-04075-HSG            Document 76          Filed 08/13/26     Page 2 of 4




                                   1   May 2025, CAET submitted a request to OFAC for a license to refund SGS’s payment. This

                                   2   request remains pending.

                                   3           Although Plaintiff originally filed this case in August 2024, Dkt. No. 1, it now seeks a

                                   4   preliminary injunction requiring Defendant “to preserve and deposit $2,000,000.00 into the

                                   5   Court’s registry,” Dkt. No. 68 at 1. Plaintiff argues that the preliminary injunction is necessary to

                                   6   preserve the status quo because “there is no assurance that the funds will remain available when

                                   7   the Court or OFAC ultimately determines the parties’ rights.” Id. at 3. Plaintiff generally asserts

                                   8   that it is “concerned that the disputed funds may be transferred, dissipated, used for other business

                                   9   operations, used to resolve other disputes, or otherwise become unavailable before final judgment

                                  10   in this action.” Id. at 8.

                                  11    II.    LEGAL STANDARD
                                  12           A plaintiff seeking preliminary relief must establish that: (1) it is likely to succeed on the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   merits; (2) it is likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of preliminary relief; (3) the

                                  14   balance of equities tips in its favor; and (4) an injunction is in the public interest. Winter v. Nat.

                                  15   Res. Def. Council, 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). Preliminary relief is “an extraordinary remedy that may

                                  16   only be awarded upon a clear showing that the plaintiff is entitled to such relief.” Id. at 22. A

                                  17   court must find that “a certain threshold showing” is made on each of the four required elements.

                                  18   Leiva-Perez v. Holder, 640 F.3d 962, 966 (9th Cir. 2011). Under the Ninth Circuit’s sliding scale

                                  19   approach, a preliminary injunction may issue if there are “serious questions going to the merits” if

                                  20   “a hardship balance [also] tips sharply towards the [movant],” and “so long as the [movant] also

                                  21   shows that there is a likelihood of irreparable injury and that the injunction is in the public

                                  22   interest.” All. for the Wild Rockies v. Cottrell, 632 F.3d 1127, 1135 (9th Cir. 2011).

                                  23           Where a plaintiff seeks mandatory injunctive relief instead of prohibitory injunctive relief

                                  24   to maintain the status quo, a plaintiff’s burden is “doubly demanding.” Garcia v. Google, Inc.,

                                  25   786 F.3d 733, 740 (9th Cir. 2015). Such a plaintiff “must establish that the law and facts clearly

                                  26   favor her position, not simply that she is likely to succeed.” Id. And the Ninth Circuit often

                                  27   cautions that a mandatory injunction “goes well beyond simply maintaining the status quo

                                  28   pendente lite [and] is particularly disfavored.” Id. (quoting Stanley v. Univ. of S. Cal., 13 F.3d
                                                                                           2
                                         Case 4:25-cv-04075-HSG            Document 76         Filed 08/13/26     Page 3 of 4




                                   1   1313, 1320 (9th Cir. 1994)). District courts therefore should deny such requests “unless the facts

                                   2   and law clearly favor the moving party.” Stanley, 13 F.3d at 1320 (quotation omitted). Put

                                   3   differently, mandatory injunctive relief should never issue in “doubtful cases.” Garcia, 786 F.3d

                                   4   at 740 (quoting Park Vill. Apartment Tenants Ass’n v. Mortimer Howard Tr., 636 F.3d 1150, 1160

                                   5   (9th Cir. 2011)).

                                   6   III.   DISCUSSION
                                   7          As an initial matter, the parties dispute whether Plaintiff is seeking a mandatory injunction.

                                   8   Compare Dkt. No. 72 at 23, with Dkt. No. 73 at 11–12. A preliminary injunction “can take two

                                   9   forms,” either a “prohibitory injunction” or a “mandatory injunction.” Marlyn Nutraceuticals, Inc.

                                  10   v. Mucos Pharma GmbH & Co., 571 F.3d 873, 878–79 (9th Cir. 2009). “Prohibitory

                                  11   injunction[s]” simply “preserve the status quo pending a determination of the action on the

                                  12   merits,” while “mandatory injunction[s]” “order[] a responsible party to take action.” Id.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   (quotation omitted). Given the weakness of Plaintiff’s motion, however, the line between

                                  14   mandatory versus prohibitory injunctions is not dispositive here. Even assuming Plaintiff is

                                  15   seeking a prohibitory injunction, it has failed to meet its burden of establishing that an injunction

                                  16   is warranted under the circumstances.

                                  17          Plaintiff does not meaningfully grapple with Defendant’s asserted defense that regulations

                                  18   currently prevent it from delivering Plaintiff the equipment or returning the payment because of its

                                  19   ties to SMIC. But even putting that aside, Plaintiff has not shown that it is likely to suffer

                                  20   irreparable harm. At bottom, Plaintiff asserts that there is a risk of dissipation, concealment, or an

                                  21   inability to recover its $2 million payment because to date Defendant has not provided a refund.

                                  22   Plaintiff also suggests that Defendant’s conduct indicates that it is generally untrustworthy and

                                  23   may not preserve the $2 million during the pendency of this litigation. In support of this

                                  24   supposition, Plaintiff asserts that Defendant’s “non-delivery, non-refund, lack of segregation,

                                  25   CAET’s exclusive control, CAET’s asserted regulatory barrier to repayment, and CAET’s refusal

                                  26   to give any assurance that the funds will remain available creates the specific risk at issue.” See

                                  27   Dkt. No. 73 at 10. But far from suggesting untrustworthiness, this list simply indicates that

                                  28   Defendant (1) has not returned Plaintiff’s $2 million because it believes it cannot do so without
                                                                                          3
                                         Case 4:25-cv-04075-HSG            Document 76        Filed 08/13/26      Page 4 of 4




                                   1   OFAC approval; and (2) has not proactively segregated the funds. This is not enough. The Court

                                   2   also notes that Plaintiff filed this case in August 2024, but waited nearly two years before filing a

                                   3   motion for preliminary injunction. Plaintiff does not cite any changed circumstances explaining

                                   4   why it waited so long to do so. Rather, it points out that “the case was delayed by CAET’s

                                   5   transfer/dismissal strategy” as well as “CAET’s motion to stay” and OFAC application. But none

                                   6   of those actions precluded Plaintiff from filing a motion for preliminary injunction. In short,

                                   7   Plaintiff has failed to show that it is entitled to the “extraordinary remedy” of a preliminary

                                   8   injunction.

                                   9   IV.    CONCLUSION
                                  10          The Court DENIES the motion. Dkt. No. 68.

                                  11          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                  12   Dated: 8/13/2026
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13                                                    ______________________________________
                                                                                        HAYWOOD S. GILLIAM, JR.
                                  14                                                    United States District Judge

 1           2.2     “CONFIDENTIAL” Information or Items: information (regardless of how it is

 3   Civil Procedure 26(c).

17           2.8     Non-Party: any natural person, partnership, corporation, association, or other legal

18   entity not named as a Party to this action.

20   but are retained to represent or advise a party to this action and have appeared in this action on

22           2.10    Party: any party to this action, including all of its officers, directors, employees,

23   consultants, retained experts, and Outside Counsel of Record (and their support staffs).

24           2.11    Producing Party: a Party or Non-Party that produces Disclosure or Discovery

25   Material in this action.

27   photocopying, videotaping, translating, preparing exhibits or demonstrations, and organizing,

28   storing, or retrieving data in any form or medium) and their employees and subcontractors.

 1          2.13    Protected Material: any Disclosure or Discovery Material that is designated as

 2   “CONFIDENTIAL.”

 3          2.14    Receiving Party: a Party that receives Disclosure or Discovery Material from a

 4   Producing Party.

 5   3.     SCOPE

 6          The protections conferred by this Stipulation and Order cover not only Protected Material (as

 7   defined above), but also (1) any information copied or extracted from Protected Material; (2) all

 8   copies, excerpts, summaries, or compilations of Protected Material; and (3) any testimony,

 9   conversations, or presentations by Parties or their Counsel that might reveal Protected Material.

10   However, the protections conferred by this Stipulation and Order do not cover the following

11   information: (a) any information that is in the public domain at the time of disclosure to a Receiving

12   Party or becomes part of the public domain after its disclosure to a Receiving Party as a result of

13   publication not involving a violation of this Order, including becoming part of the public record

14   through trial or otherwise; and (b) any information known to the Receiving Party prior to the

15   disclosure or obtained by the Receiving Party after the disclosure from a source who obtained the

16   information lawfully and under no obligation of confidentiality to the Designating Party. Any use of

17   Protected Material at trial shall be governed by a separate agreement or order.

18   4.     DURATION

19          Even after final disposition of this litigation, the confidentiality obligations imposed by this

20   Order shall remain in effect until a Designating Party agrees otherwise in writing or a court order

21   otherwise directs. Final disposition shall be deemed to be the later of (1) dismissal of all claims and

22   defenses in this action, with or without prejudice; and (2) final judgment herein after the completion

23   and exhaustion of all appeals, rehearings, remands, trials, or reviews of this action, including the

24   time limits for filing any motions or applications for extension of time pursuant to applicable law.

25   5.     DESIGNATING PROTECTED MATERIAL

26          5.1     Exercise of Restraint and Care in Designating Material for Protection. Each Party or

27   Non-Party that designates information or items for protection under this Order must take care to

28   limit any such designation to specific material that qualifies under the appropriate standards. The
                                                       3
      Case 4:25-cv-04075-HSG            Document 75          Filed 08/06/26    Page 4 of 13




 1   Designating Party must designate for protection only those parts of material, documents, items, or

 2   oral or written communications that qualify – so that other portions of the material, documents,

 3   items, or communications for which protection is not warranted are not swept unjustifiably within

 4   the ambit of this Order.

 5          Mass, indiscriminate, or routinized designations are prohibited. Designations that are shown

 6   to be clearly unjustified or that have been made for an improper purpose (e.g., to unnecessarily

 7   encumber or retard the case development process or to impose unnecessary expenses and burdens on

 8   other parties) expose the Designating Party to sanctions.

 9          If it comes to a Designating Party’s attention that information or items that it designated for

10   protection do not qualify for protection, that Designating Party must promptly notify all other Parties

11   that it is withdrawing the mistaken designation.

12          5.2      Manner and Timing of Designations. Except as otherwise provided in this Order (see,

13   e.g., second paragraph of section 5.2(a) below), or as otherwise stipulated or ordered, Disclosure or

14   Discovery Material that qualifies for protection under this Order must be clearly so designated

15   before the material is disclosed or produced.

16          Designation in conformity with this Order requires:

17                (a) For information in documentary form (e.g., paper or electronic documents, but

18   excluding transcripts of depositions or other pretrial or trial proceedings), that the Producing Party

19   affix the legend “CONFIDENTIAL” to each page that contains protected material. If only a portion

20   or portions of the material on a page qualifies for protection, the Producing Party also must clearly

21   identify the protected portion(s) (e.g., by making appropriate markings in the margins).

22   A Party or Non-Party that makes original documents or materials available for inspection need not

23   designate them for protection until after the inspecting Party has indicated which material it would

24   like copied and produced. During the inspection and before the designation, all of the material made

25   available for inspection shall be deemed “CONFIDENTIAL.” After the inspecting Party has

26   identified the documents it wants copied and produced, the Producing Party must determine which

27   documents, or portions thereof, qualify for protection under this Order. Then, before producing the

28   specified documents, the Producing Party must affix the “CONFIDENTIAL” legend to each page
                                                        4

 1   that contains Protected Material. If only a portion or portions of the material on a page qualifies for

 2   protection, the Producing Party also must clearly identify the protected portion(s) (e.g., by making

 3   appropriate markings in the margins).

 4                (b) for testimony given in deposition or in other pretrial or trial proceedings, that the

 5   Designating Party identify on the record, before the close of the deposition, hearing, or other

 6   proceeding, all protected testimony.

 7                (c) for information produced in some form other than documentary and for any other

 8   tangible items, that the Producing Party affix in a prominent place on the exterior of the container or

 9   containers in which the information or item is stored the legend “CONFIDENTIAL.” If only a

10   portion or portions of the information or item warrant protection, the Producing Party, to the extent

11   practicable, shall identify the protected portion(s).

12          5.3      Inadvertent Failures to Designate. If timely corrected, an inadvertent failure to

13   designate qualified information or items does not, standing alone, waive the Designating Party’s

14   right to secure protection under this Order for such material. Upon timely correction of a

15   designation, the Receiving Party must make reasonable efforts to assure that the material is treated in

16   accordance with the provisions of this Order.

17   6.     CHALLENGING CONFIDENTIALITY DESIGNATIONS

18          6.1      Timing of Challenges. Any Party or Non-Party may challenge a designation of

19   confidentiality at any time. Unless a prompt challenge to a Designating Party’s confidentiality

20   designation is necessary to avoid foreseeable, substantial unfairness, unnecessary economic burdens,

21   or a significant disruption or delay of the litigation, a Party does not waive its right to challenge a

22   confidentiality designation by electing not to mount a challenge promptly after the original

23   designation is disclosed.

24          6.2      Meet and Confer. The Challenging Party shall initiate the dispute resolution process

25   by providing written notice of each designation it is challenging and describing the basis for each

26   challenge. To avoid ambiguity as to whether a challenge has been made, the written notice must

27   recite that the challenge to confidentiality is being made in accordance with this specific paragraph

28   of the Protective Order. The parties shall attempt to resolve each challenge in good faith and must
                                                         5

 1   begin the process by conferring directly (in voice to voice dialogue; other forms of communication

 2   are not sufficient) within 14 days of the date of service of notice. In conferring, the Challenging

 3   Party must explain the basis for its belief that the confidentiality designation was not proper and

 4   must give the Designating Party an opportunity to review the designated material, to reconsider the

 5   circumstances, and, if no change in designation is offered, to explain the basis for the chosen

 6   designation. A Challenging Party may proceed to the next stage of the challenge process only if it

 7   has engaged in this meet and confer process first or establishes that the Designating Party is

 8   unwilling to participate in the meet and confer process in a timely manner.

 9          6.3     Judicial Intervention. If the Parties cannot resolve a challenge without court

10   intervention, the Designating Party shall file and serve a motion to retain confidentiality under Civil

11   Local Rule 7 (and in compliance with Civil Local Rule 79-5, if applicable) within 21 days of the

12   initial notice of challenge or within 14 days of the parties agreeing that the meet and confer process

13   will not resolve their dispute, whichever is earlier. Each such motion must be accompanied by a

14   competent declaration affirming that the movant has complied with the meet and confer

15   requirements imposed in the preceding paragraph. Failure by the Designating Party to make such a

16   motion including the required declaration within 21 days (or 14 days, if applicable) shall

17   automatically waive the confidentiality designation for each challenged designation. In addition, the

18   Challenging Party may file a motion challenging a confidentiality designation at any time if there is

19   good cause for doing so, including a challenge to the designation of a deposition transcript or any

20   portions thereof. Any motion brought pursuant to this provision must be accompanied by a

21   competent declaration affirming that the movant has complied with the meet and confer

22   requirements imposed by the preceding paragraph.

23          The burden of persuasion in any such challenge proceeding shall be on the Designating

24   Party. Frivolous challenges, and those made for an improper purpose (e.g., to harass or impose

25   unnecessary expenses and burdens on other parties) may expose the Challenging Party to sanctions.

26   Unless the Designating Party has waived the confidentiality designation by failing to file a motion to

27   retain confidentiality as described above, all parties shall continue to afford the material in question

28   the level of protection to which it is entitled under the Producing Party’s designation until the court

                                                         7

 1   necessary and who have signed the “Acknowledgment and Agreement to Be Bound” (Exhibit A),

10           If a Party is served with a subpoena or a court order issued in other litigation that compels

27   9.      A NON-PARTY’S PROTECTED MATERIAL SOUGHT TO BE PRODUCED IN THIS

28           LITIGATION
                                                       8

 1              (a) The terms of this Order are applicable to information produced by a Non-Party in this

15              (c) If the Non-Party fails to object or seek a protective order from this court within 14

22   10.    UNAUTHORIZED DISCLOSURE OF PROTECTED MATERIAL

23          If a Receiving Party learns that, by inadvertence or otherwise, it has disclosed Protected

21   court order secured after appropriate notice to all interested persons, a Party may not file in the
